name: Giuseppe Garibaldi
info: Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882) was an Italian general, revolutionary and republican from Nice who fought in South America and Europe, led the Expedition of the Thousand in 1860 and is remembered as a maker of Italian unification.

facts.born: 4 July 1807 in Nice, christened Joseph-Marie Garibaldi; son of Domenico Garibaldi of Chiavari and Maria Rosa Nicoletta Raimondi of Loano, a Ligurian family in the coastal trade
facts.died: 2 June 1882 on the island of Caprera, after years confined to bed by arthritis; buried on his farm there, against his wish for a simple funeral and cremation
facts.role: Commander of the Uruguayan fleet and the Italian Legion (from 1842); General of the Roman Republic (1849); major general of the Hunters of the Alps (1859); dictator of Sicily in the name of Victor Emmanuel II (1860); commander of the Army of the Vosges (1870); deputy in the Piedmontese and Italian parliaments and the French National Assembly
facts.known: the Expedition of the Thousand (1860); the defence of the Roman Republic (1849); the Redshirts; the Italian Legion in Uruguay; the meeting with Victor Emmanuel II at Teano; the march on Rome halted at Aspromonte (1862); the name "Hero of the Two Worlds"

t: A sailor from Nice drawn into Giuseppe Mazzini's Young Italy, Garibaldi was sentenced to death after a failed rising in 1834 and spent 14 years in South America, fighting for the Ragamuffins in Brazil and raising the Redshirts in Uruguay.

Back in Italy he defended the Roman Republic in 1849 and then, setting his republicanism aside for the Sardinian monarchy, led the Expedition of the Thousand in 1860, which won Sicily and Naples for the new Kingdom of Italy.

His attempts to take Rome from the pope failed at Aspromonte in 1862 and Mentana in 1867; anti-papal and later a supporter of the Paris Commune, he became an international symbol of national independence and republican ideals.
dyk: When the Union offered him a major general's commission in 1861, Garibaldi said he would serve only as commander-in-chief, with the power to declare the abolition of slavery. Lincoln was not yet ready to free the slaves, and Garibaldi did not join the Union army.
ev: Born in Nice and christened Joseph-Marie Garibaldi, into a Ligurian family in the coastal trade
Takes part in a failed Mazzinian insurrection in Piedmont; sentenced to death, he escapes and sails for South America
Takes command of the Uruguayan fleet and raises the Italian Legion, the Redshirts, for the Uruguayan Civil War
Commands the defence of the Roman Republic against the French and retreats to San Marino; his wife Anita dies near Comacchio
Leads the Hunters of the Alps against the Austrians in the Second Italian War of Independence
Leads the Expedition of the Thousand, conquers Sicily, enters Naples and greets Victor Emmanuel II as King of Italy at Teano
Marches on Rome under the slogan "Rome or Death" and is wounded and captured by government troops at Aspromonte
Dies on Caprera; he is buried on his farm there rather than cremated as he had wished

sections.early:
Giuseppe Garibaldi was born and christened Joseph-Marie Garibaldi on 4 July 1807 in Nice, to the Ligurian family of Domenico Garibaldi from Chiavari and Maria Rosa Nicoletta Raimondi from Loano. In 1814 the Congress of Vienna returned Nice to Victor Emmanuel I of Sardinia; in 1860 the Treaty of Turin would give it back to France, over Garibaldi's objections. His family's involvement in coastal trade drew him to a life at sea.

From 1828 to 1832 he lived in the Pera district of Istanbul, where he taught Italian, French and mathematics and had close ties with the Sardinian exile network in the Ottoman Empire. In April 1833 he sailed to Taganrog, in the Russian Empire, aboard the schooner Clorinda with a shipment of oranges. There he met Giovanni Battista Cuneo from Oneglia, a member of Giuseppe Mazzini's secret Young Italy movement, which sought Italian unification as a liberal republic through political and social reform.

In November 1833 Garibaldi met Mazzini in Genoa, the start of a long relationship that later became troubled. He joined the Carbonari revolutionary association, and in February 1834 he took part in a failed Mazzinian insurrection in Piedmont. He was sentenced to death but escaped, and sailed by way of the Beylik of Tunis to South America, where he spent 14 years in exile.
sections.rise:
In the Empire of Brazil Garibaldi took up the cause of the Riograndense Republic, joining the rebels known as the Ragamuffins in the war of 1835. There he met Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro da Silva, known as Anita, who fought beside him at Imbituba and Laguna in 1839. In 1841 the couple moved to Montevideo, where he worked as a trader and schoolmaster; they married the following year. In 1842 he took command of the Uruguayan fleet and raised an Italian Legion for the Uruguayan Civil War from the city's large Italian population: 4,205 of 30,000 inhabitants in an 1843 census. Allied with the Colorados of Fructuoso Rivera against Manuel Oribe's Blancos and the Argentine forces of Juan Manuel de Rosas, he defended Montevideo between 1842 and 1848 and won two victories in 1846 with amphibious guerrilla tactics.

The revolutions of 1848 brought him home with about 60 legionaries. Rebuffed by Charles Albert of Sardinia, he fought for the provisional government of Milan against Austria. In 1849 he commanded the defence of the Roman Republic, defeating a far larger French army at the Porta San Pancrazio on 30 April before the French took the city after a siege. He withdrew with 4,000 troops, hunted by Austrian, French, Spanish and Neapolitan forces; only 250 men remained when he reached San Marino, and Anita, carrying their fifth child, died near Comacchio during the retreat.
sections.deeds:
A second exile took Garibaldi to New York, where he worked in Antonio Meucci's candle factory on Staten Island, and as a merchant captain to Peru, China and Tyneside. Back in Italy in 1854, he bought half of the island of Caprera. When the Second Italian War of Independence broke out in 1859 he was appointed major general and formed the Hunters of the Alps, who beat the Austrians at Varese, Como and elsewhere. From then on he abandoned Mazzini's republican ideal, judging that only the Sardinian monarchy could free Italy.

In April 1860 uprisings in Messina and Palermo gave him his chance. With the Thousand he sailed from Quarto, in Genoa, on 5 May and landed at Marsala on 11 May. At Calatafimi on 15 May he led 800 volunteers to victory over 1,500 with an uphill bayonet charge, and the next day he declared himself dictator of Sicily in the name of Victor Emmanuel II. Palermo surrendered after a siege and a truce arranged by a British admiral, and he won the hard Battle of Milazzo.

Crossing the Strait of Messina, he entered Naples by train on 7 September. At the Volturno on 30 September his 24,000 volunteers could not decisively defeat about 25,000 Neapolitans; his largest battle was settled by the arrival of the Royal Sardinian Army. At Teano on 26 October he greeted Victor Emmanuel as King of Italy, and he retired to Caprera, refusing any reward. The Kingdom of Italy was created on 17 March 1861.
sections.opponents:
In 1845, during the Anglo-French blockade of the Río de la Plata, Garibaldi led what are remembered as the infamous sacks of Martín García island and Gualeguaychú. Of Sicily in 1860, historians Clough et al. argue that his volunteers were students, artisans and professionals rather than peasants; the peasants who backed him acted out of hatred of exploitive landlords and Neapolitan officials, and Garibaldi, who had no interest in social revolution, sided with the landlords against the rioting peasants.

His chief rival on his own side was Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, whose realpolitik he mistrusted and whom he attacked in parliament in April 1860 for ceding Nice to Napoleon III. Cavour in turn feared that Garibaldi would invade the Papal States and bring French intervention. Garibaldi was intensely anti-Catholic and anti-papal; Catholics around the world viewed his hostility to the pope's temporal power with distrust, and he was excommunicated. In 1862 he raised volunteers under the slogan "Rome or Death" against the government's wishes. On 28 August regular troops met them at Aspromonte; Garibaldi forbade his men to return fire, and he was wounded in the foot and imprisoned.

In 1867 he told the League of Peace and Freedom that the papacy "ought to be abolished", and in 1875 he urged "the oppressed of Eastern Europe" to drive "the Turk" back to Broussa. Denis Mack Smith judged that socialism meant nothing very revolutionary to him, and that he perhaps flaunted the word partly to shock the Mazzinians.
sections.last:
In 1866, with the full support of the Italian government, Garibaldi led some 40,000 Hunters of the Alps into the Trentino and defeated the Austrians at Bezzecca. After the regular forces' defeats at Custoza and Lissa, an armistice gave Venetia to Italy, largely because of Prussia's successes, and he was ordered to halt short of Trento. He replied by telegram: Obbedisco! ("I obey"). In 1867 he marched on Rome again; the Papal army, supported by a French force, defeated his badly armed volunteers at Mentana, where he was shot in the leg, and the government imprisoned him once more.

When the Second French Empire collapsed in 1870 he took the side of the new Government of National Defense, commanded the volunteer Army of the Vosges and was elected to the French National Assembly. In 1871 he declared his full support for the Paris Commune and called the First International "the sun of the future". Elected again to the Italian parliament, he spent much of his late years on Caprera; in 1879 he founded the League of Democracy with Felice Cavallotti, Alberto Mario and Agostino Bertani, for universal suffrage and the emancipation of women.

Ill and confined to bed by arthritis, he married Francesca Armosino, with whom he already had three children, in 1880. He died on Caprera on 2 June 1882, his bed moved so that he could see the sea. His wishes for a simple funeral and cremation were not respected.
sections.legacy:
Garibaldi's popularity, his skill at rousing the common people and his military exploits are credited with making the unification of Italy possible. He is counted with Cavour, Victor Emmanuel II and Mazzini among Italy's "fathers of the fatherland", and twentieth-century historiography and popular culture regard him as Italy's greatest national hero. Uruguay still celebrates him as a contributor to its reconstitution.

Abraham Lincoln, Victor Hugo, Charles Dickens and Friedrich Engels were among those who praised him, and he inspired Jawaharlal Nehru and Che Guevara. A. J. P. Taylor called him "the only wholly admirable figure in modern history"; Denis Mack Smith wrote that at the height of his glory he was perhaps the most famous person in Italy. G. M. Trevelyan's trilogy of 1907–11 portrayed him, in David Cannadine's words, as a Carlylean hero whose inspired leadership created the Italian nation. His religious convictions are unclear to historians: in 1882 he wrote that "Man created God, not God created Man", yet his autobiography has him call himself a good Christian.

Five ships of the Italian Navy, a Polish legion of the January Uprising and a French legion of the First World War took his name, and statues of him stand in Rome, Nice, Buenos Aires and elsewhere. In 2012 his descendants announced plans to exhume his remains for DNA analysis; they were sidelined in 2013.

summary: Giuseppe Garibaldi (1807–1882), a general and republican from Nice, fought in the wars of Brazil and Uruguay before returning to Italy. His Expedition of the Thousand in 1860 won Sicily and Naples for Victor Emmanuel II, and he is counted among Italy's "fathers of the fatherland", though his marches on Rome failed.

notes: The article does not say who ruled Nice in 1807, only that the Congress of Vienna returned it to Sardinia in 1814; nothing is said of 1807 beyond the birth.
The death sentence (1834) is in the article's lead only; the Early life section gives just the failed insurrection.

The article says contemporary sources do not mention the Redshirts in Uruguay and that their origin there is popular history; the takeaway uses the name as the article's lead does ('raising an Italian force known as Redshirts').
Rome's capture without him (1870) and the Volturno decided by the Royal Sardinian Army are given as the article gives them.

Left out for space: Freemasonry (initiated 1844, later Grand Master of the Grand Orient of Italy), the 1847 letter to Pius IX, the Pacific voyages in detail, the marriage of 1860 to Giuseppina Raimondi, the American Civil War letter of 1863, the Garibaldi Guard, Mount Garibaldi, Nottingham Forest's colours and the other commemorations.
The article quotes Garibaldi's 1875 letter on the Ottomans at length; only its call to drive 'the Turk' to Broussa is given, in the opponents section.
